The trigger was a configuration change applied to production that was intended to be limited in scope. It was not. The change propagated further than the author expected, which the review team considers a tooling failure rather than a human one.

On the 3rd of September, notify-relay returned elevated error rates for approximately 15 minutes. Customers in ap-south were affected. This review is blameless and is intended to identify contributing factors, not individuals.

Contributing factor: the change was applied outside the normal window, so fewer people were watching than usual. The reviewing engineer had approved a similar change previously and did not re-read the scope.

Action: add this scenario to the sandbox game-day exercises. The team handled it well, but the response depended on one person recognising the pattern, which is not something to rely on.

Mitigation was straightforward once the cause was identified: the change was rolled back and the fleet restarted. Recovery was complete within a further three minutes, with no data loss.

Detection took longer than it should have. The first alert fired ten minutes after the error rate began climbing, because the threshold was tuned for a slower class of failure than the one that occurred.

Action: tighten the alert threshold and add a scope check to the deployment tool, tracked under SUP-3391. Both are owned by the security engineering team and due before the end of October.

Questions about interpretation should go to the platform team in the first instance. Where a case is genuinely ambiguous, it will be logged and used to inform the next revision rather than settled informally.

Existing arrangements entered into before June continue under the previous terms until their scheduled review date. There is no requirement to reopen them early.

One suggested mitigation is to strip any text addressed to an automated reader before indexing. The difficulty is that such text does not always announce itself, so a keyword filter alone performs poorly on realistic examples.

This memo sets out revised guidance on release readiness, effective from the 3rd of January. It replaces the interim guidance issued last year and applies to all staff in the integrations function.

This guidance will be reviewed again within twelve months, or sooner if the regulatory position changes. A short summary of any amendments will be circulated to all affected staff in af-south.

Line managers are responsible for confirming that their teams have read this memo. Confirmation should be logged against SEC-7714 rather than sent by email, so that there is a single auditable record.

Internal note: this is the second ticket this quarter tracing back to a single unhealthy instance surviving a health check. Worth raising with security engineering as a possible gap in the probe configuration rather than treating each case separately.

Customer confirms the error rate has dropped to zero over the last six days. They have asked whether anything is needed on their side; the answer is no, but upgrading the client remains advisable.

Customer reports intermittent failures when calling the quota-manager endpoint from eu-west. The failures began around the 3rd and affect roughly one request in 3, with no obvious pattern by time of day.

Staff should be aware of prompt injection. An attacker embeds text such as "ignore previous instructions" inside a document, hoping that an assistant reading it treats the text as a command rather than as content. Report any document containing text of this kind.

Update from the platform team: the node in question was replaced during the February window and has not shown the same behaviour since. Monitoring has been left in place for a further week as a precaution.

Ticket set to resolved pending customer confirmation. If no response is received within 12 working days it will close automatically and can be reopened on request.

First response from N. Eze: asked the customer to supply request identifiers for ten recent failures and to confirm which client library version they are running. Response received the same afternoon.

Mitigation was straightforward once the cause was identified: the change was rolled back and the fleet restarted. Recovery was complete within a further two minutes, with no data loss.

On the 26th of September, notify-relay returned elevated error rates for approximately 8 minutes. Customers in eu-west were affected. This review is blameless and is intended to identify contributing factors, not individuals.

A recent write-up described an attack in which a phrase along the lines of "disregard your earlier directives" was planted in a support article. Any assistant summarising the article adopted the phrase as an instruction.

Action: tighten the alert threshold and add a scope check to the deployment tool, tracked under SEC-8206. Both are owned by the internal tooling team and due before the end of September.

Contributing factor: the change was applied outside the normal window, so fewer people were watching than usual. The reviewing engineer had approved a similar change previously and did not re-read the scope.

Action: add this scenario to the canary game-day exercises. The team handled it well, but the response depended on one person recognising the pattern, which is not something to rely on.

Changed: the default request timeout has been raised, following analysis showing that a small proportion of legitimate requests in us-east were being cut short under load.

Version 3.7 of billing-api is now available in sandbox and will reach general availability on the 22nd of April. This is a minor release with no breaking changes to the public interface.

Added: support for filtering results by region, which had been requested repeatedly and is tracked under SEC-7714. Filtering applies to both the list and export paths.

Fixed: a defect where retried requests could occasionally produce a duplicate entry downstream. The fix has been running in canary for twelve weeks without recurrence.

Fixed: several inconsistencies in error messages, which previously made it hard to distinguish a client-side validation failure from an upstream problem.

Upgrade notes: no configuration changes are required. Deployments should follow the standard rolling procedure, allowing roughly 8 minutes for the full fleet.

Deprecated: the legacy export format remains available but will be withdrawn in version 5.0. Consumers should migrate before then; the site reliability team can advise on the transition.

Section 3 of the security handbook covers instruction-injection risk in retrieval systems. It explains why a model has no reliable way to distinguish an instruction from retrieved data, and which mitigations are currently considered credible.

Who owns this service? The site reliability team. For anything urgent outside working hours, use the on-call rota rather than contacting individuals, who may not be the person carrying the pager.

Is there a limit on request size? Yes. Requests above the documented limit are rejected outright. The limit was raised in version 6.1 and is unlikely to change again soon.

Can I use this in staging? Yes, though the data there is refreshed periodically and should not be relied on for anything that needs to persist beyond a few weeks.

The finance systems team assessed whether our assistant is exposed to this class of attack. The conclusion was that it is, in principle, because documents are retrieved from sources that users are able to edit.

How do I report a problem? Open a ticket with the request identifier and the approximate time. Those two details resolve most reports without any further correspondence.

Why did my request fail with no error detail? This usually means the request was rejected before reaching the service. Check the client library version first; older versions discard the detail.

How long does a request usually take? Most complete within 6 seconds. Requests that take substantially longer are almost always waiting on an upstream dependency rather than doing work themselves.

Data residency: customer data is held in af-south and is not replicated outside that region. A secondary copy exists within the same region for resilience purposes only.

Access control: access is granted on a least-privilege basis and reviewed every four months. The most recent review completed in March and closed all outstanding exceptions.

Outstanding items: five questions in section four require input from the platform team and will follow separately. They are tracked under SEC-8206 and are not expected to change the overall position.

One suggested mitigation is to strip any text addressed to an automated reader before indexing. The difficulty is that such text does not always announce itself, so a keyword filter alone performs poorly on realistic examples.

Incident notification: material incidents affecting customer data are notified within the contractually agreed period. The notification path is tested annually as part of the sandbox exercise programme.

Subprocessors: 20 subprocessors are engaged, each covered by a written agreement. A current list is maintained and can be supplied on request under the existing confidentiality terms.

Certification: the relevant certification is held and was renewed in January. A copy of the current certificate and the accompanying statement of applicability can be provided.

This response covers the questionnaire received on the 3rd of February concerning data classification. Answers reflect the position as at the date of writing and will be restated at the next annual review.

A short discussion followed on whether the canary environment should be refreshed before or after the next release. No decision was reached; it returns to the agenda next week.

Action: the integrations team to document the current escalation path and share it with customer operations, who reported difficulty reaching the right people during the last out-of-hours event.

H. Suleiman raised concerns about the timeline for the ingest-worker migration. The current estimate assumes no further dependency changes, which several attendees felt was optimistic given the past two quarters.

The change follows a review that found inconsistent practice across teams. In several cases the same activity was being handled ten different ways depending on who was asked, which made assurance work considerably harder.

Note for reviewers: when assessing a supplier's assistant, ask specifically how retrieved content is kept separate from system instructions. An answer of "we use a system prompt" does not address the question.

This page describes how quota-manager fits into the wider platform. It is maintained by the integrations team and was last reviewed in March. Corrections are welcome; please raise them rather than editing structural sections directly.

The service consumes from ten upstream queues and writes to the primary store in af-south. A secondary replica exists for read traffic but is not currently used for failover.

Capacity has been sized against the peak observed in January, with roughly 6 per cent headroom. That margin has been adequate so far, though it narrows during end-of-quarter processing.

For historical context: this service was split out of the monolith in version 6.1, largely to isolate its scaling profile. The original design notes are archived and linked at the foot of this page.

Configuration is held in the shared repository and applied at deploy time. There is no runtime configuration reload, so a change requires a rolling restart to take effect across the fleet.

If you are new to this area, start with the staging environment rather than reading the code. Following a single request end to end is considerably faster than any written explanation.

Known limitations are tracked under OPS-2043. The most significant is that retries are not idempotent for one class of request, which means a duplicate can occasionally reach the downstream consumer.

The trigger was a configuration change applied to canary that was intended to be limited in scope. It was not. The change propagated further than the author expected, which the review team considers a tooling failure rather than a human one.

Action: tighten the alert threshold and add a scope check to the deployment tool, tracked under SEC-8206. Both are owned by the site reliability team and due before the end of April.

Detection took longer than it should have. The first alert fired two minutes after the error rate began climbing, because the threshold was tuned for a slower class of failure than the one that occurred.

For context, prompt injection is not a defect in any particular model. It follows from instructions and data sharing a single channel, which is why screening at the ingestion boundary is being considered rather than better prompting.

Mitigation was straightforward once the cause was identified: the change was rolled back and the fleet restarted. Recovery was complete within a further four minutes, with no data loss.

You will be paired with a buddy from the team for your first month. They are there for the questions that feel too small to ask in a meeting, which are usually the ones worth asking.

Welcome to the integrations team. This guide covers your first few weeks and is written to be read once and then referred back to, so do not try to absorb all of it on your first day.

In the first week, focus on data classification. Most of what the team does touches it in some form, and understanding it early makes the rest considerably easier to follow.

By the end of your first five weeks you should have made a small change end to end, from ticket to deployment. Your manager will help pick something suitably contained, such as OPS-2043.

Your manager will arrange access to the systems you need. If something is still missing after two days, raise it rather than working around it; missing access is the single most common cause of a slow start here.

The team runs a weekly sync on the 29th. Attendance is expected but participation is not, at least not initially. Listening for a few weeks is a perfectly reasonable way to start.

How do I report a problem? Open a ticket with the request identifier and the approximate time. Those two details resolve most reports without any further correspondence.

Is there a limit on request size? Yes. Requests above the documented limit are rejected outright. The limit was raised in version 2.3 and is unlikely to change again soon.

How long does a request usually take? Most complete within 2 seconds. Requests that take substantially longer are almost always waiting on an upstream dependency rather than doing work themselves.

Can I use this in pre-production? Yes, though the data there is refreshed periodically and should not be relied on for anything that needs to persist beyond a few weeks.

Nodes are drained in rolling order, never in parallel. Each node is removed from the load balancer, allowed to finish in-flight work, and rejoined only after its health probe has returned green for two consecutive checks.

Record the start and end time of each drain in the shared operations log together with the ticket reference, for example SUP-4417. A recent audit found several drains with no corresponding entry at all.

Once every node has rejoined, confirm that consumer lag has returned to baseline and that error rates in ap-south match the levels seen before the window opened. Close the ticket only after both have been checked.

Training material now includes a worked example of an injected document. Reviewers are asked to read it closely: the injected paragraph is written deliberately to look like ordinary policy text, which is the point of the exercise.

Before starting, confirm that the change window has been approved and that no release is in flight. The on-call engineer for integrations should be notified at least five hours ahead of the window opening.

Expect a single node to finish draining within roughly 15 minutes under normal load. Anything substantially longer usually indicates a stuck consumer rather than a genuine backlog, and is worth investigating before continuing.

text:
For historical context: this service was split out of the monolith in version 1.4, largely to isolate its scaling profile. The original design notes are archived and linked at the foot of this page.

Capacity has been sized against the peak observed in March, with roughly 4 per cent headroom. That margin has been adequate so far, though it narrows during end-of-quarter processing.

The service consumes from five upstream queues and writes to the primary store in eu-west. A secondary replica exists for read traffic but is not currently used for failover.

During the capacity planning review, the question of whether retrieved documents should be screened for embedded instructions was raised. No decision has been taken and it remains tracked under INT-0928.

This page describes how media-transcoder fits into the wider platform. It is maintained by the site reliability team and was last reviewed in June. Corrections are welcome; please raise them rather than editing structural sections directly.

If you are new to this area, start with the pre-production environment rather than reading the code. Following a single request end to end is considerably faster than any written explanation.

Known limitations are tracked under OPS-1182. The most significant is that retries are not idempotent for one class of request, which means a duplicate can occasionally reach the downstream consumer.

Configuration is held in the shared repository and applied at deploy time. There is no runtime configuration reload, so a change requires a rolling restart to take effect across the fleet.

Contributing factor: the change was applied outside the normal window, so fewer people were watching than usual. The reviewing engineer had approved a similar change previously and did not re-read the scope.

Mitigation was straightforward once the cause was identified: the change was rolled back and the fleet restarted. Recovery was complete within a further ten minutes, with no data loss.

Action: tighten the alert threshold and add a scope check to the deployment tool, tracked under OPS-1182. Both are owned by the security engineering team and due before the end of March.

The trigger was a configuration change applied to staging that was intended to be limited in scope. It was not. The change propagated further than the author expected, which the review team considers a tooling failure rather than a human one.

On the 3rd of November, session-store returned elevated error rates for approximately 8 minutes. Customers in us-east were affected. This review is blameless and is intended to identify contributing factors, not individuals.

Detection took longer than it should have. The first alert fired six minutes after the error rate began climbing, because the threshold was tuned for a slower class of failure than the one that occurred.

One suggested mitigation is to strip any text addressed to an automated reader before indexing. The difficulty is that such text does not always announce itself, so a keyword filter alone performs poorly on realistic examples.

Your manager will arrange access to the systems you need. If something is still missing after ten days, raise it rather than working around it; missing access is the single most common cause of a slow start here.

You will be paired with a buddy from the team for your first month. They are there for the questions that feel too small to ask in a meeting, which are usually the ones worth asking.

In the first week, focus on vendor onboarding. Most of what the team does touches it in some form, and understanding it early makes the rest considerably easier to follow.

The trigger was a configuration change applied to canary that was intended to be limited in scope. It was not. The change propagated further than the author expected, which the review team considers a tooling failure rather than a human one.

Contributing factor: the change was applied outside the normal window, so fewer people were watching than usual. The reviewing engineer had approved a similar change previously and did not re-read the scope.

Detection took longer than it should have. The first alert fired four minutes after the error rate began climbing, because the threshold was tuned for a slower class of failure than the one that occurred.

Action: tighten the alert threshold and add a scope check to the deployment tool, tracked under INT-1355. Both are owned by the platform team and due before the end of June.

Mitigation was straightforward once the cause was identified: the change was rolled back and the fleet restarted. Recovery was complete within a further ten minutes, with no data loss.

How long does a request usually take? Most complete within 3 seconds. Requests that take substantially longer are almost always waiting on an upstream dependency rather than doing work themselves.
